# Draft:Tokara Leaf Warbler

| genus = Phylloscopus
| species =
| authority = (Saitoh et al., 2026)
}}
The Tokara leaf warbler is a recently described cryptic species of Old World warbler in the family Phylloscopidae. It is endemic to the Tokara Islands in the Nansei Shoto archipelago of Japan. Previously considered an undifferentiated, geographically isolated population of Ijima's leaf warbler (Phylloscopus ijimae), it was formally recognized as a distinct species to science in 2026 based on deep genetic divergence and distinct vocalizations.
Taxonomy
The population of leaf warblers on the Tokara Islands was first discovered relatively recently, in 1988, on the island of Nakanoshima. For decades, they were believed to be the same species as Ijima's leaf warbler, which breeds roughly 1,000 km away in the Izu Islands.
In 2026, a comprehensive study analyzing DNA demonstrated a deep phylogenetic split. The genetic divergence between the Tokara and Izu populations is estimated to have occurred roughly 2.8 to 3.2 million years ago, a divergence deeper than that seen between over 30 other widely recognized species of leaf warblers. The data suggests a complete lack of recent or contemporary gene flow between the two populations, likely driven by strong innate philopatry (the tendency to return to exact breeding grounds) despite overlapping migration routes.
Description
The Tokara leaf warbler is a classic cryptic species, meaning it is morphologically nearly identical to its sister species. Researchers found no noticeable plumage differences between the Tokara and Izu populations. Morphometric analysis showed minimal physical differentiation, with the only statistically significant differences found in tarsus length and total head length.
Because they are visually indistinguishable, vocalizations serve as a primary differentiator. The song of the Tokara leaf warbler is markedly distinct. Both species utilize two main types of songs (Type I and Type II), but the Tokara's Type I song differs significantly in all measured acoustic variables. In discriminant function analyses, 100% of the Tokara recordings were correctly classified apart from Izu recordings based on song alone. Conversely, their short contact calls do not show significant differences.
Distribution and habitat
The breeding range of the Tokara leaf warbler is highly restricted. While singing males have been observed during the breeding season on five small islands in the Tokara archipelago (including Kuchinoshima, Suwanosejima, and Akusekijima), confirmed breeding has only been recorded on Nakanoshima. Genetic sampling of birds on autumn migration through southern Kyushu suggests the birds travel south along the island chain to wintering grounds in the Philippines.
Conservation
The authors of the species description proposed that the Tokara leaf warbler should be classified as Vulnerable (VU) on the IUCN Red List and retain the "Natural Monument" designation in Japan.
The species faces critical threats due to its small, geographically restricted island habitat. Recent surveys have failed to find the bird on Tairajima, an island where it was previously observed. Known threats on the islands include predation by introduced Japanese weasels (Mustela itatsi) and severe habitat modification caused by domestic goats.
Population genomics indicate that the Tokara leaf warbler has very low genetic diversity and short runs of homozygosity, reflecting historical population bottlenecks and a history of inbreeding. However, genomic assessments also show a low "deleterious load" (the proportion of highly harmful genetic mutations), suggesting the population has successfully purged many harmful alleles over time and retains evolutionary resilience.
